M01:
*If you have been here before,* the landing is as you left it, and behind the yellow letters the beeping hasn't stopped. Go straight to the choices.

*If this is your first time at this section,* Level 5 smells of Milton and toast. The landing opens onto a square of lino with the nurses' station in the middle of it: a hip-high counter, a desk, a hook of keys, a cream phone ringing to itself.

On the left, double doors with a stork painted on the frosted glass: MATERNITY. On the right, WARD 9, the doors papered with sugar-paper animals, a giraffe with its neck gone soft from being leant on. You were born behind one set of doors and very nearly stopped, aged eight, behind the other.

Next to the lift there is a second stairwell door. It isn't on any floor below this one. Somebody has stencilled it in the same tacky yellow as the line downstairs: WARD 0 - CLOSED.

Behind it, a monitor is beeping. You know the rhythm before you know you're listening. Steady, steady, and every eleventh beat or so a little skip, the one the GP calls an ectopic and Mum calls her hiccup. You have lain awake listening for that skip through a bedroom wall for six years.

If you haven't looked at the book lying open on the station counter, turn to {M02}.

If you haven't answered the phone on the nurses' station, it is still ringing. Turn to {M08}.

If you haven't been through to the delivery suite, turn to {M14}.

If you haven't been onto Ward 9, turn to {M18}.

If you have not already tried the door marked WARD 0, and you open it and go to the monitor, turn to {D08}.

If you have THE LAST RULE, you can take the stairs back down to the Main Corridor. Turn to {M28}.

If you do not have THE LAST RULE, you can still go back down without it. Turn to {M29}.
M02:
The book on the counter is a ledger the size of a paving slab, bound in green cloth gone black at the corners where thumbs have held it. Gold letters on the spine: DELIVERIES 1991.

A biro lies in the gutter, lid missing, the end chewed flat. The pages are ruled in columns: DATE, TIME, MOTHER, AGE, BABY, WEIGHT, MIDWIFE, REMARKS. Every entry is in a different hand, and every one is in ink.

The last entries ought to be on the thirty-first of December. They aren't. The book goes on past the new year, page after page, and the paper at the back is whiter than the paper at the front. It's been forced flat at the back, the spine cracked open there, where somebody has been writing lately.

Near the front, the paper is softer. One page has been turned so often that its corner has gone to felt.

*If Ros is with you,* she looks at the book without touching it. 'Ninety-one,' she says. 'I was four. I remember a yellow coat and being sick in Dad's Cortina on the way here.' She keeps her hands in her pockets.

If you turn to March 1991, turn to {M03}.

If you turn to the last page, the one with tonight's date on it, turn to {M04}.
M03:
The soft page is March. You run your finger down the dates until it stops on its own.

14.3.91   01:47
MOTHER: Maureen DOYLE   AGE: 36
BABY: live birth, cried straight off
WEIGHT: 7lb 2oz
MIDWIFE: J. Pickering
REMARKS: Mother asked for tea and toast. Then more toast. Laughed through second stage. Apologised to student midwife for language (twice).

It's a midwife's hand, round and quick, and you can hear Mum in every line of it. You can hear the student midwife too, nineteen and scarlet.

Taped into the margin, the tape gone the colour of weak tea, is a band of white plastic small enough to fit round two of your fingers. The card inside it says, in blue biro: BABY OF MAUREEN. 14.3.91. 01:47.

That's all it says. No name, no ward, no next of kin. You were nobody's but hers yet.

Thirty-six. She was a year older than you are now. Your birth certificate has the date on it and nothing else. You were never told the minute. It turns out to be a minute like any other, with somebody living through it at the end of a long night, asking for toast.

Lose 1 Fear.

*If Ros is with you,* she reads it upside down and laughs once, through her nose, at *(twice)*. 'She told me she was a model patient,' she says. 'She told me that for years.'

You leave the book open at March. Turn to {M01}.
M04:
The last page has the same columns, but someone has written across the top of them in capitals, pressing hard: ADMISSIONS.

Tonight's date runs down the left-hand side. The names next to it are in ink, a dozen hands from a dozen decades: copperplate, a schoolgirl's loops, a biro that skipped. Every BED column is filled in.

At the bottom, the last line is your name. It's in pencil, in a neat upright hand with every letter joined. The BED column beside it is empty. The pencil has been left light, to be gone over in ink once it's certain.

You lick your thumb and rub it out.

It doesn't come off clean. Pencil never does. You rub until the grey goes to a smear and the smear goes to nothing and the paper under your thumb is thin enough to see the station light through.

When you take your thumb away, the letters are still there, pressed into the page, readable if you tilt it. In the gutter, the biro has its lid back on.

Gain 1 Fear.

Turn to {M01}.
M08:
The phone on the nurses' station is cream plastic gone the colour of old piano keys, with a curly cord and a row of clear buttons along the bottom for the lines. One of them is lit. A Dymo label on the handset says WARD 9 NIGHTS.

It rings the old way, two rings and a gap. It has been ringing since you came up the stairs, and nobody has come.

Beside it is a mug of tea gone cold with a skin on it, and on the rim a half-moon of lipstick, coral, the shade Mum has worn to every wedding and every funeral since you can remember.

You stand by the counter with your hand an inch above the receiver. You have answered a lot of phones since the first stroke. GP surgery, pharmacy, the stroke nurse, the woman from the council about the rail in the bath. You know the way a ring sounds when it's bad news. This one just sounds patient.

*If Ros is with you,* she checks her own phone first: no signal, the bars an empty staircase. 'Leave it,' she says. Then: 'No. Answer it. If it's theatre—' She doesn't finish the sentence.

If you answer it, turn to {M09}.

If you let it ring, turn to {M01}.
M09:
The receiver smells of somebody else's hand cream. A long hiss, a clatter of crockery a long way off, and then a voice you would know through a wall.

'Bean? It's tomorrow here. Don't ask.'

It's Mum. Hoarse, slurred at the edges, cross. 'They've had a tube down me. I sound like a docker. There's a nurse here about twelve years old and she's given me a jelly. Green. I ask you.'

You say *Mum*. It comes out of you without any breath behind it.

'Course it's me. Who else rings you at this hour?' Then she says your name. Your real one, all of it, the one on your birth certificate, the one she uses when you're in trouble or when she's proud of you and can't think how else to say it.

*If at least one field of your Wristband is filled,* the band under your sleeve stops itching. You turn your cuff back. Whatever the hospital last wrote on it, she has just said something over the top of it, and the plastic there is clean. Cross off 1 field on your Wristband.

*Otherwise,* there is nothing on your wrist for her to wipe, and the voice goes through you anyway, with nowhere to land. Lose 2 Fear.

'Has your sister said owt?' Mum says.

*If you have the codeword SPOKE:* 'About Toronto? I sent her, you know. Packed her off. She'll not have said. She's like me, she'd sooner—' The line crackles over the end of it. When it clears she's still talking, quieter. 'I asked you to stay,' she says, 'which I'd no business doing.'

*Otherwise,* the line crackles over whatever comes next, and does not give it back.

*If you have the codeword MENDED,* you know. Ros told you, and you told her. 'She said,' you tell Mum. 'We both did.' A pause, and then her laugh, the filthy one, worn thin by the tube. 'About bloody time.'

'Listen,' Mum says. 'The bit I tore off. It's in the drug cupboard, love. Behind the controlled drugs. Sister never looked there. She had the only key, and she trusted herself.'

Somewhere behind her, a young voice: 'Mo, you're not meant to be on that.'

'I'm on the phone to my—'

Then hiss, and then the dialling tone, plain and flat, an ordinary Thursday noise. Turn to {M10}.
M10:
You put the receiver down. Then you pick it up again, to be sure. Dialling tone. You put it down.

The drug cupboard is on the wall behind the station: grey steel, two locks, and a red label with CONTROLLED DRUGS on it in white. Through the slatted vent in the door you can see a second cupboard inside the first, smaller, with a lock of its own.

It's locked. You try the handle anyway, because you are Mum's child.

The keys hang on a hook beside it, under the station clock. A big ring of them on a leather fob worn shiny: brass ones, steel ones, a Yale, a little one for a padlock, a long old-fashioned one with a hollow barrel that hasn't opened anything since the fifties. Twenty at least. Maybe thirty.

Out on Ward 9, footsteps. They stop at each bed, and start again.

*If Ros is with you,* she's already read the label and the locks. 'Two locks, inner cabinet, logged keys,' she says, low. 'Whoever holds those signs for every dose. They'd be the first thing she checks.' She doesn't tell you not to.

If you take the keys and try them, turn to {M11}.

If you leave them on the hook, turn to {M01}.
M11:
The ring is heavier than it looks. You lift it off the hook as quietly as you can, and every key on it moves.

The first one doesn't fit. The second goes in and won't turn. The third turns halfway and sticks, and you have to work it back out a millimetre at a time. You hold the ring in your fist to stop them chiming against each other. They chime anyway.

On the ward, the footsteps stop at a bed. Start again. Stop at the next. Each stop is a little closer to the doors.

The outer cupboard opens on the seventh key. The inner one has a smaller lock, brass, and there are a dozen small brass keys on the ring.

Test your Fortune.

If you are Lucky, turn to {M12}.

If you are Unlucky, turn to {M13}.
M12:
The ninth small key turns, and the inner door swings out on a sigh of old hinges.

Boxes of ampoules, a register with a pen on a string, a brown glass bottle with a label typed on a typewriter. You move them aside one at a time and put each one back where it was. Flat against the back panel, held there by nothing, is a strip of laminated card.

You know the type and the lamination. It's the Notice's, from the linen cupboard on Level 3, and the top edge is ragged where somebody tore it off. One line:

8. LET THEM GO.

You turn it over. On the back, in biro, there's a consultant, you can tell by the bow tie, with his trousers round his ankles and a speech bubble: WHO'S HAD MY NOTES. Under it, an M, the one off every birthday card you've had, its middle stroke dipping right down to the line. And: 1979.

You laugh. Out loud, on Level 5, in the middle of the night. You can't help it.

*If you already have THE LAST RULE,* this is a second strip, the same type, the same ragged top, as if the hospital had printed her mistake more than once. Do not note it again. *Otherwise,* note THE LAST RULE.

You lock both doors and hang the keys back on the hook. They're still swinging when the footsteps come out through the ward doors, and stop, and go back in.

*If Ros is with you,* she looks at the drawing and snorts. 'That's Mum,' she says. 'That is completely Mum. I'm having that framed.'

Turn to {M01}.
M13:
One of the small brass keys sticks. You twist it, and the whole ring jumps in your hand and every key on it chimes.

She's there.

You didn't hear the ward doors. The red torch is pointing at the floor, politely, so as not to get in your eyes. Starched cap, silver buckle, the fob watch pinned upside down. She is smiling the way you'd smile at a child up past their bedtime.

'Can't sleep?'

She takes the keys out of your hand. You let her. She picks the stuck one out of the lock without looking at it, and hangs the ring back on its hook, and the keys go still all together.

Then she lifts your wrist, and turns your cuff back with one finger, and unhooks the biro from her watch chain. In the BED field she writes a 3, small and upright.

'Bed 3,' she says, writing it. 'By the window. You always did like the window.'

*If you have been on Ward 9,* you know exactly why. *Otherwise,* you don't know why she'd say that. Not yet.

'There,' she says. 'You'll be wanting to lie down, not wander about. I'll have it made up for you.'

Fill in 1 more field on your Wristband: BED.

She goes back to her round, and the ward doors take her without a sound.

Turn to {M01}.
M14:
Through the doors with the stork on them there's a corridor of side rooms, all dark except one. DELIVERY 2. The door has a round window in it.

Inside, four theatre staff in green gowns and paper masks stand round an empty delivery bed. The stirrups are up. The gas-and-air is on its stand with the mouthpiece hooked over the top. Under the heat lamp, a little perspex cot is waiting with a folded towel in it.

They aren't doing anything. They're waiting, the way people wait at the arrivals gate, all facing the bed.

You look at their masks, and then you look properly. The paper holds the shape of a face, nose and chin, the ties pulled tight at the back of each head. Round the edges of the masks, where there should be cheek and jaw, you can see the tiles of the far wall.

One of them has a strip of card pinned to its gown with a nappy pin, the big sort with a pink plastic head. You can read the first character from here. It's an 8.

The clock over the door says 01:46. The second hand is stuck on the twelve, trembling.

*If Ros is with you,* she has the scissors out of her bag already, held low. 'Four of them,' she breathes. 'One door. I'd rather we didn't.'

If you fight them for the card, turn to {M15}.

If you slip along the wall and take it, turn to {M16}.

If you back out quietly, turn to {M01}.
M15:
The masks turn towards you, all four together, with a dry rustle of paper.

They come round the bed, unbothered. Their gloved hands are white with talc, and they hold them up and out, the way a midwife does, to show you they're clean. They want you on the bed. They want to help you up into the stirrups and settle you, and wait with you.

You get your back against the gas-and-air stand and shove the nearest one. Its mask crumples under your palm with nothing behind it, and fills again as you take your hand away.

THEATRE STAFF   NERVE 8   VIGOUR 9

If you win, the one with the card folds down into its own gown, and there's nothing on the floor but green cotton, a paper mask and a strip of card on its pink nappy pin. You snatch it up and go. Turn to {M17}.

If your Vigour reaches 0, turn to {D_VIGOUR}.
M16:
You stay low and go along the wall, past the sharps bin and the trolley with the speculums laid out in rows. The lino squeaks under your shoes. You stop. The masks don't turn.

The one with the card is nearest the cot. You come up behind it, close enough to smell the gown: autoclave, talc, and something underneath like boiled sweets. The nappy pin is through the gown and through the corner of the card, and closed.

You'll have to open it with your fingers an inch from its back.

Test your Nerve.

If you succeed, the pin opens with a tiny click and the card slides into your hand, the open pin still through its corner. Turn to {M17}.

If you fail, your thumb slips, and the pin snaps shut again on nothing. Four masks turn to look at you. Turn to {M15}.
M17:
You're out in the corridor with the card in your hand and the nappy pin still through one corner of it.

It's a strip of laminated card, torn ragged along the top where it came off something bigger. The type is the Notice's, from the linen cupboard on Level 3. One line:

8. LET THEM GO.

You read it twice. The second time, behind you in DELIVERY 2, the clock gives a clunk, and you know without going back to look that the minute hand has moved on to 01:47.

The heat lamp over the cot goes out. Nobody in the room makes a sound.

*If you already have THE LAST RULE,* this is a second strip, the same type, the same ragged top, as if the hospital had printed her mistake more than once. Do not note it again. *Otherwise,* note THE LAST RULE.

You take the pin out and close it and put it in your pocket too. It seems wrong to leave it.

*If Ros is with you,* she has her back against the delivery-room door, holding it shut, though nothing is pushing on it. She reads the card over your shoulder, her lips moving. 'That's it?' she says. 'That's the whole rule? Three words?'

Turn to {M01}.
M18:
*If you have been here before,* Ward 9 is as you left it: the rows of sleeping children, the bed by the window, the chair. Go straight to the choices.

*If this is your first time at this section,* the doors with the paper animals swing shut behind you, and it's 1999.

You know it by the telly on its bracket, CITV gone to a test card, and the Teletubbies frieze along the wall at child height. You know it by the smell, Calpol and floor polish and Wotsits. On the lockers there are Game Boys and a Furby and a Tamagotchi on a chain.

The beds run down both sides in rows, and there are children in them, asleep and smiling. Not all of them are from 1999. A girl in a liberty bodice in an iron cot. A boy with a calliper strapped over his blanket. A baby in a Babygro with poppers, in a perspex box on legs.

The bed by the window is Bed 3. The board over it has your name on, in green felt tip, with a smiley face that a nurse called Debbie drew because you asked.

And beside it, the chair. Wooden arms, a vinyl seat split down the middle and mended with brown parcel tape. A bottle-green cardigan hung over its back with a tissue up the sleeve.

You were eight. You had pneumonia in both lungs and an oxygen mask that smelled of the inside of a new paddling pool. Mum slept in that chair for a week. She went home once, to shower, and was back before you woke.

*If Ros is with you,* she stops just inside the doors. 'I came up once,' she says. 'Saturday, with Dad. I stood there.' She points at the foot of the bed. She doesn't go any nearer.

If you sit in the chair, turn to {M19}.

If you lie down in your old bed, turn to {D07}.

If you walk the ward, turn to {M23}.

If Ros is with you, and you haven't yet been into the parents' room across the corridor, turn to {M25}.

If you leave Ward 9 without sitting down, turn to {M01}.
M19:
The vinyl sighs when you sit. The parcel tape crackles under you. It's lower than you remember, and harder, and too upright to sleep in.

She slept in it anyway. Head down on her arm on the edge of the mattress, feet up on the bed frame, her coat over her for a blanket. You woke once at three and she was awake too, watching the numbers on the little monitor clipped to your finger, saying them under her breath.

This was her view, then. The bed, at the height of your face. The window, and in it the car park lights in fog, the same as tonight. Her own hands on the wooden arms, which have gone pale in two places where somebody gripped them for a week.

And from down here, where nobody standing would see it, something tucked under the mattress edge. The sheet is folded hospital-tight, and in the fold, just showing, is a corner of white card.

If you do not have THE LAST RULE, and you reach under the mattress, turn to {M20}.

If Ros is with you, and you get up and give her the chair, turn to {M21}.

If you get up and leave the ward, turn to {M01}.
M20:
You work it out from under the sheet with two fingers. It's a strip of laminated card, folded in four, small enough to hide in a fist. The lamination has cracked white along the folds.

You open it out. The Notice's type, the Notice's ragged top edge:

8. LET THEM GO.

On the back, in biro, in Mum's writing, the M with the middle stroke dipping to the line:

*Ward 9. 1999. Not yet. M.*

You remember the Wednesday. The curtains going round in the afternoon and staying round. A doctor you hadn't seen before, and then another one. The mask pressed down harder. Mum in the chair, talking to you the whole time about nothing, about the dinner-hall ladies and who'd fallen out with who over the custard.

You remember waking up on the Thursday, and Mum laughing at something on the telly.

She'd carried this for twenty years by then. She put it under you while you slept, folded small, with the words facing the mattress.

Note THE LAST RULE.

*If Ros is with you,* she reads the back over your shoulder, and for once she doesn't photograph anything. 'Wednesday,' she says. 'Dad sat up all Wednesday night by the phone in the hall. He never told me why.'

Turn to {M01}.
M21:
You get up. Ros looks at the chair as if it's a structure somebody has told her is safe and she doesn't believe them.

'I was at home,' she says. 'With Dad. You know that.'

You did know. You had never thought about it.

'I made the tea. Every night that week.' She says it in her site-report voice. 'Fish fingers, potato waffles, beans. It was the one thing I could do that didn't burn. Dad said it was lovely every night. He didn't eat it.'

'I rang the ward payphone at seven. Mum would come out to it and say you were fine. So I told Dad you were fine. And Nana. And Mrs Kerrigan next door, and my form tutor, and the girls at school.' She stops. 'I could do *fine* in my sleep.'

She has never sat in this chair. Mum was in it, the one time she came up.

She sits.

It creaks under her. She puts her hands on the wooden arms, on the two pale places, and her fingers fit them, and she takes them off again and holds them in her lap.

If you have the codeword SPOKE but not MENDED, and you tell her what that week was like for you, turn to {M22}.

If you do not have THE LAST RULE, and you reach under the mattress, turn to {M20}.

If you get up, both of you, and leave the ward, turn to {M01}.
M22:
So you tell her.

The mask that smelled of paddling pools. The Tamagotchi that would have died in the night if Mum hadn't kept it going, pressing its buttons with her thumbnail at three in the morning so you'd wake up to it alive. Mum doing the voices off *Coronation Street* until the nurse told her to pack it in.

The Wednesday. The curtains going round.

Ros listens with her hands in her lap. She doesn't get her phone out. When you've finished, she looks at the bed for a while.

'She sent me,' she says. 'Toronto.'

*If you began this in the chapel,* 'Later,' she said. This is later.

She tells you. 'At the wake. The Legion kitchen, while you were out front doing the cups. She'd had my offer letter out of my handbag and read it. She stood at the sink with her hat still on and she said:'

*If you are her daughter:* 'Go. Take the job. If you stay, your sister will let you do everything and never have a life.'

*If you are her son:* 'Go. Take the job. If you stay, your brother will let you do everything and never have a life.'

*If neither:* 'Go. Take the job. If you stay, our kid will let you do everything and never have a life.'

Ros's voice is perfectly level. 'So I went. And I let you think I'd just gone.'

Then you tell her yours, because it's the only fair thing. 'After the stroke. The second night, on the stroke unit. She got her good hand round my wrist. She said, *Stay with me. Don't let them put me anywhere.*'

'So she asked you.'

'And she sent you.'

Ros laughs. It comes out wet, and she lets it. 'She's been running us like a dinner queue,' she says. 'For eight years. Both ends.'

Lose 2 Fear. Note the codeword MENDED.

If you do not have THE LAST RULE, and you reach under the mattress, turn to {M20}.

If you get up, turn to {M01}.
M23:
You walk down the middle of the ward, between the rows.

The children sleep with their faces turned up and their hands on top of the blankets, the way nurses used to arrange them.

At the end of every bed hangs a chart on a clipboard. Temperature, pulse, respirations, every hour, in the same neat upright hand. The readings don't change from hour to hour. Perfect, perfect, perfect, back to the war.

The girl in the liberty bodice is smiling in her sleep. Her chart starts in 1952.

At the far end of the ward, a red light comes on.

It moves bed by bed. It stops at each one, and a hand lifts a small wrist into the light and holds it there, counting, and puts it back under the blanket. Then the light comes on to the next bed.

You've spent the night a room ahead of her. Now she's in this one.

If you get behind the curtains of the nearest empty bay, turn to {M24}.

If you are wearing the TABARD, you can fall in beside her and do the round. Turn to {M18}.
M24:
You step into the empty bay and draw the curtain round on its rail, as slowly as you can. The hooks tick along one at a time.

The curtain is the old sort, flowered, washed so often the flowers have gone to ghosts. You stand in the middle of the bay, away from the bed, and don't breathe.

The footsteps come. They stop on the other side of the curtain.

Her shadow is on the cloth, tall, with the corners of the cap standing out sharp. The torch comes through the flowers, red, and finds the outline of your hand where it's pressed flat against your leg.

She counts. Under her breath, a full minute by the watch on her chest. You know what she's counting. Your breaths.

At sixty, she makes a small satisfied sound, the sound of a nurse whose patient is doing nicely. The torch goes off. The footsteps move on to the next bed.

You stay where you are a long time after they've gone.

Gain 1 Fear.

Turn to {M18}.
M25:
Across the corridor from Ward 9 there's a door with a laminated sign: PARENTS' ROOM. Inside, a fold-down bed hinged to the wall, a kettle with a ring of limescale at the waterline, a jar of Nescafé, a saucer of sugar sachets. A second sign over the bed:

PARENTS MAY SLEEP HERE. PLEASE STRIP BED AFTER USE.

Ros sits down on the bed. It's already folded down and made up, the sheet turned back.

She bends and starts to unlace her boots, the Blundstones she flew in. Her fingers aren't working properly. She has been awake for a day and a half, through two time zones and a surgeon.

'Ten minutes,' she says. 'I mean it.'

She sets a timer on her phone and holds it up so you can see it: 10:00. Then she gets one boot off and sits there with it in her hand, looking at the pillow.

It's a ward bed. It's in a parents' room, with a sign that says she's allowed, and it's a ward bed.

If you take the boot out of her hand and make her stand up, turn to {M26}.

If you let her have ten minutes, turn to {M27}.
M26:
You take the boot out of her hand. Then you take her by both wrists and pull, and she comes up off the bed, surprised, in one sock.

'You are unbelievable,' she says.

Behind her, the fold-down bed lifts itself back into the wall on its hinges, slow and smooth, and clicks shut. The sheet and pillow go up with it. There's a line of dust along the skirting where it stood.

Ros doesn't see. She's looking at you.

She takes the boot back and puts it on, and laces it, double knot, the way Dad taught both of you on the back step. Then the other one. Then she stands, properly.

*If you have the codeword SPOKE,* for one second she leans her whole weight on you, her forehead against your shoulder.

Then she gets her phone out and cancels the timer.

*If you have the codeword SPOKE:* 'One, I'm not tired,' she says. 'Two, I'm tired. Three, thank you. Don't make a thing of it.'

*Otherwise:* 'Don't make a thing of it,' she says.

Note the codeword HELD.

Turn to {M18}.
M27:
You fill the kettle at the little sink. While it boils you find two mugs, a Silver Jubilee one with the handle glued and one that says WORLD'S BEST NAN. You make Ros's with milk and no sugar, the way she's taken it since she was fifteen.

The kettle clicks off. Behind you, a soft sound: hinges.

When you turn round with the mugs, the bed is folded away. The room smells of 1952: wool blanket, carbolic, coal smoke on cold air. Under the folded bed, side by side against the wall, are her boots. The laces are still undone.

The timer on her phone would have gone off by now. You can't hear it.

You put her mug down. You ring her mobile from yours, and against the odds it connects. Down the line, a long way off, a ward at night: a trolley wheel squeaking, somebody coughing the way nobody has coughed since penicillin.

Then a voice, soft and low. 'Old Wing. She's sleeping, love. Don't you fret. I'll tell her you rang.'

The line doesn't go dead. It goes back to ringing, and keeps ringing, somewhere beyond the swing doors four floors down.

Note the codeword WARDED.

Turn to {M18}.
M28:
You take the stairs down, with the strip of card in your pocket and your hand on it.

At the top landing you look back. Through the round window in the Ward 9 doors, the lights are going to night setting, one bank at a time, from the far end towards you.

You go down a flight. Level 4. The fire door there has a window too, and behind it the lights are going down, bank by bank, as you pass. Level 3. The same. The round is a room behind you all the way, and it doesn't hurry, and it doesn't fall back.

Behind the WARD 0 door, as you left, the beeping went on. Steady, steady, skip.

The stairwell smells of cigarettes from 1979 and, faint underneath, Milton and toast. You don't stop on the landings.

Gain 1 Fear.

M29:
You take the stairs down without it.

The beeping follows you. You hear it through the wall of the stairwell on the turn below Level 5: steady, steady, skip. Mum's hiccup. You go down another flight, and it's there on the landing at Level 4, no fainter. It must be the same wall all the way down.

Halfway to Level 3, it stops.

Between beats. Not on the skip. Just a gap where the next one should be.

You stand on the stairs with your hand on the rail and wait for it. You count, the way you've counted through the bedroom wall at home. Six. Seven. Twelve.

It doesn't come. Or the wall is too thick here. You tell yourself the wall is too thick here, and you go on down.

D07:
You take your shoes off first. You don't know why. Mum always made you.

The bed is a child's bed, and it fits you. It shouldn't. Your feet don't reach the end. The pillow is the old foam sort in a plastic cover that crackles under the cotton, and it smells of Calpol.

The lights go down to night setting.

Someone comes and stands over you. Someone tucks the blanket in, down one side and across the bottom and up the other, pulling it under the mattress tight, the way Mum did, so tight you can't turn over and don't want to. A hand smooths your hair off your forehead.

'Night night,' she says. 'Sleep tight.'

The voice is almost right. The hand is cool, and Mum's hands were never cool, not once, not even after the freezer at work.

It isn't Mum. You know that, and the blanket is tucked too tight to move, and the knowing doesn't help. A biro scratches at your Wristband. Rule 3 was the one about the bed.

D08:
The door opens easily. Behind it there are stairs going down, concrete, painted green, and the beeping comes up them. Steady, steady, skip. Mum's monitor, somewhere below.

You take them two at a time.

The door shuts behind you with a soft pneumatic sigh. You don't look back. You go down a flight, and turn, and go down another, and the beeping is exactly as loud as it was at the top.

There are no floor numbers on the landings. There are no doors. The stairs keep going, and so does the beeping, steady, skip, never nearer.

You go down for a long time. Your legs go, and you sit on a step to rest them, just for a minute, and listen to Mum's heart below you.

When you look at your Wristband, the WARD field is filling itself in. One figure, in yellow paint: 0.

Rule 5 said Ward 0 was closed. It didn't say what to.
